title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 9.2.1 Reading: Intensive Reading (Narratives)

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Intensive reading means reading a narrative carefully so that you understand the facts and the feelings in it. In this sub-strand you will read an original story of 320 words, learn its vocabulary, answer questions that are written on the page and questions that need clues, and put the events in order. The story is made up for learning. It shows how facts and kindness belong together.

## Strand 9.0: HIV and AIDS
Sub-strand 9.2.1: Reading: Intensive Reading (Narratives)
Suggested lessons: 3

## What this sub-strand covers
• Narratives

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 9.0 HIV and AIDS, Sub-strand 9.2.1 Intensive Reading: Narratives

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) read a short narrative of about 320 words for comprehension
b) apply appropriate reading strategies to read a narrative of about 320 words for information
c) appreciate reading for purposes of comprehension and information

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why do we read narratives?
2. What makes you enjoy reading a narrative?

PAGE 2: How we will learn

## Learning experiences
• read a passage in print or non-print format and answer questions
• discuss vocabulary from the passage and use them to construct simple sentences
• answer factual and inferential questions from a passage collaboratively
• give the sequence of events in a given story or passage
• read a digital text online or offline and collaborate in answering questions with peers

## Core competencies
• Communication and Collaboration: This is enhanced as the learner answers factual and inferential questions in groups.
• Self-efficacy: This is achieved when the learner answers inferential and factual questions correctly.

## Values
• Love: It is nurtured when the learner respects others as they read texts online or offline and answer questions.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Clubs and Societies: Reading clubs, writing clubs, journalism clubs among others build the learner’s self-esteem to become more confident readers as they manoeuvre to give the sequence of events in a story.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner can link the content obtained from the theme of HIV and AIDS to concepts taught in Agriculture and,Science and Technology.

PAGE 3: Lesson 1: Reading for facts and new words

LESSON 1: READING FOR FACTS AND NEW WORDS
=========================================

## What you will learn
• Read a narrative of 320 words carefully.
• Work out the meaning of new words from the story.
• Answer factual questions in your own words.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read a short narrative of about 320 words for comprehension; b) apply appropriate reading strategies to read a narrative of about 320 words for information

## Introduction
A story can teach a fact without looking like a chart. If you race, you may remember only that someone was unkind. If you read closely, you can say exactly what was said, what was true and what changed.

PAGE 4: Lesson 1: Reading for facts and new words — How to read closely

## Notes

### How to read closely
Before you read, look at the title and ask what it might mean. During reading, follow four questions: Who is here? Where are they? What happens? Which words are new? After reading, check whether you can answer without looking, then look back to confirm.

When a word is unfamiliar, read the whole sentence again. Whispered sits beside a boy who does not want to be heard. The sentence tells you the meaning. Then try the word in a new sentence of your own.

A factual question is answered by words in the text. You do not have to guess. Use a short sentence and, if you can, the name of the person who did the action.

PAGE 5: Lesson 1: Reading for facts and new words — A Place at the Desk

### A Place at the Desk
The narrative below has 320 words.

On Monday a new girl called Amina joined our class. She smiled, set her bag down and asked if she could sit beside me. I said yes. At break she skipped faster than anyone, and we laughed together.

On Tuesday I heard two boys by the tap. One whispered that we should not share a bottle with Amina because someone in her home was living with HIV. The other boy pulled his bottle away. Amina was near the door. She heard every word. She ate her lunch alone under the tree.

Our class teacher, Mr Okello, noticed. On Wednesday he did not shame anyone. He said we were going to learn facts, because a story that is only half heard can hurt a person. The school nurse, Sister Wairimu, came with a chart. She told us that HIV is a virus. It can pass through blood, for example when people share a razor blade or a needle that has fresh blood on it. It does not pass through a handshake, a desk, a pencil, a cup or a game. You cannot tell that someone has HIV by looking at their face.

PAGE 6: Lesson 1: Reading for facts and new words — Notes 5

Sister Wairimu added that there is no cure yet, but medicine helps people living with HIV stay well. They go to school, play and work when they take that medicine as the doctor advises. She said a long cough should be checked at a clinic, because an illness such as tuberculosis needs its own medicine. A cough does not mean a person has HIV.

I walked to Amina and said I was sorry, and that she should sit with us. She nodded. Her auntie takes her medicine and is strong, and Amina is strong too. On Friday we wrote a class promise. We sit with everyone, we do not tease anyone about illness, and we never share sharp objects. Amina led the skipping again, and the whole class cheered.

PAGE 7: Lesson 1: Reading for facts and new words — Words from the narrative

### Words from the narrative
- **whispered**: spoke very quietly, so that not everyone was meant to hear.
- **virus**: a tiny germ. HIV is a virus.
- **cure**: a treatment that ends an illness. The nurse says there is no cure yet for HIV.
- **medicine**: something given by a doctor or nurse to treat or control an illness.
- **tuberculosis**: an illness that is not HIV. It needs its own medicine.
- **promise**: a serious agreement you intend to keep.
- **tease**: to mock someone. The class promise says they will not tease anyone about illness.

This story is imagined for the lesson. Do not treat it as news about a real family, and do not spread talk about a real person's health.

PAGE 8: Lesson 1: Reading for facts and new words — Example 2

## Key words
• intensive reading — reading carefully for meaning, not only to finish the page
• factual question — a question whose answer is stated in the text
• whisper — to speak very quietly
• promise — a serious agreement you mean to keep

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Who came to class with a chart?

Working:
1. Look for the word chart.
2. The sentence says the school nurse, Sister Wairimu, came with a chart.

Answer: Sister Wairimu

## Worked examples

### Example 2
According to the nurse, does a cough mean a person has HIV?

Working:
1. Find the sentence about a cough.
2. It says a cough does not mean a person has HIV.

Answer: No

PAGE 9: Lesson 1: Reading for facts and new words — Read and prove it

## Activity: Read and prove it
You will need: The narrative A Place at the Desk, Notebook

1. Read the narrative silently. Mark any word you cannot yet explain.

2. In pairs, choose three of those words and agree on a meaning from the sentences around them.

3. Write three factual questions and swap them with another pair.

4. Answer by pointing to the sentence that proves you are right.

## Practice

1. On which day did Amina join the class?

2. What reason did the boy give for not sharing a bottle?

3. Name two things Sister Wairimu said do not pass HIV.

4. What did the class promise about sharp objects?

PAGE 10: Lesson 2: Inferences and the order of events

## Answers to practice

1. Monday

2. He said someone in Amina's home was living with HIV.

3. Any two: a handshake, a desk, a pencil, a cup or a game.

4. They promised never to share sharp objects.

## Summary
• Close reading asks who, where, what and which words are new.
• A factual answer can be proved by a sentence in the story.
• The narrative is imagined, and real people's health is not for gossip.

LESSON 2: INFERENCES AND THE ORDER OF EVENTS
============================================

## What you will learn
• Answer questions that need a clue from the narrative.
• Put the events of the story in order.
• Explain a character's feeling using evidence.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read a short narrative of about 320 words for comprehension; b) apply appropriate reading strategies to read a narrative of about 320 words for information

## Introduction
The story never says Amina was sad in those exact words. It says she ate her lunch alone under the tree. A careful reader can move from that clue to a fair conclusion.

PAGE 11: Lesson 2: Inferences and the order of events — Inference

## Notes

### Inference
An **inference** is a conclusion you draw from clues. The text gives you the clue. You add what you know about how people act, and you stay fair. You do not invent a new plot.

Clue: Amina heard the boys, then ate alone. Inference: she was hurt and did not feel welcome. That fits the text. It would not be fair to infer that she was ill, because the story gives no such fact. Sister Wairimu says you cannot tell that someone has HIV by looking at their face, and the story never says Amina herself has HIV.

More clues:
- Mr Okello did not shame anyone. He wanted facts, not a quarrel.
- The narrator said sorry and offered a seat. The narrator knew the talk at the tap had been wrong.
- On Friday the whole class cheered. The welcome had changed.

A good answer uses both parts: the clue and the conclusion. Amina ate alone, so I think she felt left out.

PAGE 12: Lesson 2: Inferences and the order of events — Sequence

### Sequence
**Sequence** means the order of events. Time words in this story are the days of the week.

1. Monday: Amina joins the class, sits with the narrator and skips with the others.
2. Tuesday: two boys whisper by the tap, and Amina eats alone.
3. Wednesday: Mr Okello and Sister Wairimu teach the facts.
4. After that talk: the narrator apologises, and Amina explains that her auntie takes medicine and is strong.
5. Friday: the class writes a promise, and Amina leads the skipping while everyone cheers.

If you put Friday before Tuesday, the promise appears before the hurt, and the story stops making sense. A sequence chart with one box for each day keeps the order visible.

PAGE 13: Lesson 2: Inferences and the order of events — Example 1

Read the narrative again before you answer. Intensive reading often means a second and third reading, each time with a sharper question. The first reading gives the shape. The second gives the clues.

## Key words
• inference — a fair conclusion drawn from clues in the text
• sequence — the order in which events happen
• clue — a detail in the text that helps you work something out

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Why is it unfair to say that Amina has HIV?

Working:
1. Search the story for a sentence that says Amina has HIV.
2. There is none. The boys talk about someone in her home, and even that talk is gossip.
3. The nurse says you cannot tell by looking.

Answer: The story never says Amina has HIV. Guessing from gossip or from her appearance would be unfair and incorrect.

PAGE 14: Lesson 2: Inferences and the order of events — Day by day

## Worked examples

### Example 2
What happened just after the nurse's lesson, and before Friday?

Working:
1. The lesson is on Wednesday.
2. The next paragraph is the apology.
3. Friday is the promise.

Answer: The narrator apologised and asked Amina to sit with the class.

## Activity: Day by day
You will need: Five cards labelled Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, After the talk, Friday, The narrative

1. Reread the narrative with a partner.

2. Write one event on each card and arrange the cards in order.

3. Answer two inference questions together: Why did Amina eat alone? Why did the narrator apologise?

4. For each answer, underline the clue you used in the story.

PAGE 15: Lesson 2: Inferences and the order of events — Answers to practice

## Practice

1. What clue shows that Amina was hurt by the talk at the tap?

2. Why did Mr Okello avoid shaming the boys?

3. Put these events in order: the promise, the whisper, Amina joining the class.

4. What can you infer from the whole class cheering on Friday?

## Answers to practice

1. She heard every word and then ate her lunch alone under the tree.

2. He wanted the class to learn facts, because a half-heard story can hurt someone.

3. Amina joining the class, then the whisper, then the promise.

4. The class had welcomed Amina again and was glad to play with her.

## Summary
• An inference joins a clue from the text to a fair conclusion.
• Do not add facts the story does not support.
• The days of the week give the sequence of this narrative.

PAGE 16: Lesson 3: Why we read narratives — Information and understanding

LESSON 3: WHY WE READ NARRATIVES
================================

## What you will learn
• Explain how a narrative can carry both feelings and information.
• Use a simple way to remember what you have read.
• Show respect when you discuss a text with others.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply appropriate reading strategies to read a narrative of about 320 words for information; c) appreciate reading for purposes of comprehension and information

## Introduction
You could learn the same health facts from a poster. The story does something extra: it lets you stand beside Amina at the tap and decide what you would say. That is a good reason to read narratives.

## Notes

### Information and understanding
We read narratives for enjoyment and for information. Enjoyment comes from wanting to know what happens next and from caring about the people in the story. Information in this narrative includes facts a nurse would want a class to remember: HIV is a virus, it is not passed by sharing a bottle, medicine helps people stay well, and tuberculosis is a different illness.

A story can make those facts easier to remember because they are tied to a person and a day. You may forget a lonely list. You are more likely to remember that the bottle was pulled away and that the nurse corrected the fear.

PAGE 17: Lesson 3: Why we read narratives — Ways to keep what you read

### Ways to keep what you read
- Retell the story in five sentences, one for each stage.
- Write three new words and use each one in a sentence that is not copied from the book.
- Ask one factual question and one inference question, then answer both.
- Talk about the story in a reading club. Listen to other readers. Their favourite moment may not be yours, and that is useful.

If you read the narrative on a screen, stay on the text your teacher has opened. Do not type a classmate's name or health into a chat, a comment or a message. This story is made up. A real person's health is private.

PAGE 18: Lesson 3: Why we read narratives — Example 1

### Respect while you talk
Kind discussion sounds like this: I think Amina wanted a friend, because she asked to sit down on Monday. It does not sound like a joke about illness. Love, in this lesson, is practical. It is a seat saved, an apology said, and a promise kept.

Reading is worth the effort when it leaves you better informed and more able to treat people fairly. Close the book and ask, What do I know now that I did not know at the title? If you can answer, the reading has done its work.

## Key words
• retell — to tell a story again in your own words and in the right order
• reading club — a group that meets to read and talk about texts
• private — not for public talk or for posting online

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Give one fact and one feeling a reader can take from the narrative.

Working:
1. A fact is something the nurse states.
2. A feeling is shown by what a character does.

Answer: Fact: HIV is not passed by sharing a cup or a bottle. Feeling: Amina was hurt when she heard the boys, because she ate alone.

PAGE 19: Lesson 3: Why we read narratives — Five sentences and a promise

## Worked examples

### Example 2
Why is it wrong to post a classmate's health online after a lesson like this?

Working:
1. Health is private.
2. The class story was a warning against gossip.

Answer: A person's health is private. Posting it would spread gossip, which the story shows can hurt someone.

## Activity: Five sentences and a promise
You will need: The narrative, in print or on a screen the teacher has chosen, Exercise books

1. With a partner, retell the story in five sentences, using Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, after the talk and Friday.

2. Each learner writes one new sentence using the word promise and one using the word virus.

3. In a small group, share what you enjoyed in the story and one fact you will remember. Listen without interrupting.

4. Agree on one way your own class can welcome a new learner.

PAGE 20: Lesson 3: Why we read narratives — Answers to practice

## Practice

1. Give two reasons to read a narrative.

2. How can a story help you remember a fact?

3. What should you not type online after reading this story?

4. What question can you ask yourself to check that reading was useful?

## Answers to practice

1. For enjoyment and for information.

2. The fact is tied to a character and an event, so it is easier to recall than a bare list.

3. A real classmate's name or health, or gossip about a person's illness.

4. What do I know now that I did not know before I read the title?

## Summary
• Narratives give enjoyment and information together.
• Retelling, new sentences and careful talk help you remember.
• Real people's health is private and is not material for jokes or posts.

PAGE 21: Revision quiz

REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. How many words is the narrative A Place at the Desk?
   A. About 60
   B. About 120
   C. 320
   D. 3,000

2. Where did Amina eat lunch on Tuesday?
   A. Beside the narrator
   B. Alone under the tree
   C. In the nurse's room
   D. At the tap with the two boys

3. What did Sister Wairimu say about a cure for HIV?
   A. There is no cure yet
   B. A special fruit is the cure
   C. A haircut is the cure
   D. Sharing a bottle cures it

4. Tuberculosis in the story is ________.
   A. another name for HIV
   B. a different illness that needs its own medicine
   C. a kind of razor
   D. a game

5. Why did Amina eat alone? The best answer uses a clue.
   A. The story says she was not hungry
   B. She heard unkind talk and no longer felt included
   C. The nurse told her to sit under the tree
   D. She wanted to read a chart

6. Which event happened first?
   A. The class wrote a promise
   B. Amina joined the class
   C. Sister Wairimu brought a chart
   D. The narrator apologised

7. It is unfair to decide that Amina has HIV because ________.
   A. the story says so in the first line
   B. the story never says that, and you cannot tell by looking
   C. she skipped faster than anyone
   D. her auntie takes medicine, so Amina must be ill

8. What did the narrator do after the nurse's lesson?

9. Why are narratives worth reading, according to this sub-strand?

10. What is one safe way to remember the story?

PAGE 22: Quiz answers

ANSWERS
=======

1. C. 320
   The lesson narrative is 320 words long, the length this sub-strand asks you to read.

2. B. Alone under the tree
   After she heard the boys, she ate her lunch alone under the tree.

3. A. There is no cure yet
   She said there is no cure yet, but medicine helps people stay well.

4. B. a different illness that needs its own medicine
   The nurse says tuberculosis needs its own medicine and that a cough does not mean a person has HIV.

5. B. She heard unkind talk and no longer felt included
   She heard every word by the door, and the next sentence shows her eating alone.

6. B. Amina joined the class
   Amina joined on Monday, before the whisper, the lesson and the apology.

7. B. the story never says that, and you cannot tell by looking
   Gossip about her home is not proof about Amina, and the nurse says you cannot tell by looking at a face.

8. The narrator apologised and asked Amina to sit with the class.
   The paragraph after the lesson begins with the apology.

9. They give enjoyment and information, and they help us understand how other people feel.
   A story can carry facts and feelings together.

10. Retell it in order, or write new sentences with the new words, without posting anyone's private health information.
   Remembering the text is useful. Gossip about real people is not.

## Activity: Read and prove it
You will need: The narrative A Place at the Desk, Notebook

1. Read the narrative silently. Mark any word you cannot yet explain.

2. In pairs, choose three of those words and agree on a meaning from the sentences around them.

3. Write three factual questions and swap them with another pair.

4. Answer by pointing to the sentence that proves you are right.

## Practice

1. On which day did Amina join the class?

2. What reason did the boy give for not sharing a bottle?

3. Name two things Sister Wairimu said do not pass HIV.

4. What did the class promise about sharp objects?

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Inferences and the order of events
studyPages.body:
## Answers to practice

1. Monday

2. He said someone in Amina's home was living with HIV.

3. Any two: a handshake, a desk, a pencil, a cup or a game.

4. They promised never to share sharp objects.

## Summary
• Close reading asks who, where, what and which words are new.
• A factual answer can be proved by a sentence in the story.
• The narrative is imagined, and real people's health is not for gossip.

LESSON 2: INFERENCES AND THE ORDER OF EVENTS
============================================

## What you will learn
• Answer questions that need a clue from the narrative.
• Put the events of the story in order.
• Explain a character's feeling using evidence.

Curriculum outcomes: a) read a short narrative of about 320 words for comprehension; b) apply appropriate reading strategies to read a narrative of about 320 words for information

## Introduction
The story never says Amina was sad in those exact words. It says she ate her lunch alone under the tree. A careful reader can move from that clue to a fair conclusion.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Inferences and the order of events — Inference
studyPages.body:
## Notes

### Inference
An **inference** is a conclusion you draw from clues. The text gives you the clue. You add what you know about how people act, and you stay fair. You do not invent a new plot.

Clue: Amina heard the boys, then ate alone. Inference: she was hurt and did not feel welcome. That fits the text. It would not be fair to infer that she was ill, because the story gives no such fact. Sister Wairimu says you cannot tell that someone has HIV by looking at their face, and the story never says Amina herself has HIV.

More clues:
- Mr Okello did not shame anyone. He wanted facts, not a quarrel.
- The narrator said sorry and offered a seat. The narrator knew the talk at the tap had been wrong.
- On Friday the whole class cheered. The welcome had changed.

A good answer uses both parts: the clue and the conclusion. Amina ate alone, so I think she felt left out.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Inferences and the order of events — Sequence
studyPages.body:
### Sequence
**Sequence** means the order of events. Time words in this story are the days of the week.

1. Monday: Amina joins the class, sits with the narrator and skips with the others.
2. Tuesday: two boys whisper by the tap, and Amina eats alone.
3. Wednesday: Mr Okello and Sister Wairimu teach the facts.
4. After that talk: the narrator apologises, and Amina explains that her auntie takes medicine and is strong.
5. Friday: the class writes a promise, and Amina leads the skipping while everyone cheers.

If you put Friday before Tuesday, the promise appears before the hurt, and the story stops making sense. A sequence chart with one box for each day keeps the order visible.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Inferences and the order of events — Example 1
studyPages.body:
Read the narrative again before you answer. Intensive reading often means a second and third reading, each time with a sharper question. The first reading gives the shape. The second gives the clues.

## Key words
• inference — a fair conclusion drawn from clues in the text
• sequence — the order in which events happen
• clue — a detail in the text that helps you work something out

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Why is it unfair to say that Amina has HIV?

Working:
1. Search the story for a sentence that says Amina has HIV.
2. There is none. The boys talk about someone in her home, and even that talk is gossip.
3. The nurse says you cannot tell by looking.

Answer: The story never says Amina has HIV. Guessing from gossip or from her appearance would be unfair and incorrect.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Inferences and the order of events — Day by day
studyPages.body:
## Worked examples

### Example 2
What happened just after the nurse's lesson, and before Friday?

Working:
1. The lesson is on Wednesday.
2. The next paragraph is the apology.
3. Friday is the promise.

Answer: The narrator apologised and asked Amina to sit with the class.

## Activity: Day by day
You will need: Five cards labelled Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, After the talk, Friday, The narrative

1. Reread the narrative with a partner.

2. Write one event on each card and arrange the cards in order.

3. Answer two inference questions together: Why did Amina eat alone? Why did the narrator apologise?

4. For each answer, underline the clue you used in the story.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Inferences and the order of events — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. What clue shows that Amina was hurt by the talk at the tap?

2. Why did Mr Okello avoid shaming the boys?

3. Put these events in order: the promise, the whisper, Amina joining the class.

4. What can you infer from the whole class cheering on Friday?

## Answers to practice

1. She heard every word and then ate her lunch alone under the tree.

2. He wanted the class to learn facts, because a half-heard story can hurt someone.

3. Amina joining the class, then the whisper, then the promise.

4. The class had welcomed Amina again and was glad to play with her.

## Summary
• An inference joins a clue from the text to a fair conclusion.
• Do not add facts the story does not support.
• The days of the week give the sequence of this narrative.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Why we read narratives — Information and understanding
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: WHY WE READ NARRATIVES
================================

## What you will learn
• Explain how a narrative can carry both feelings and information.
• Use a simple way to remember what you have read.
• Show respect when you discuss a text with others.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply appropriate reading strategies to read a narrative of about 320 words for information; c) appreciate reading for purposes of comprehension and information

## Introduction
You could learn the same health facts from a poster. The story does something extra: it lets you stand beside Amina at the tap and decide what you would say. That is a good reason to read narratives.

## Notes

### Information and understanding
We read narratives for enjoyment and for information. Enjoyment comes from wanting to know what happens next and from caring about the people in the story. Information in this narrative includes facts a nurse would want a class to remember: HIV is a virus, it is not passed by sharing a bottle, medicine helps people stay well, and tuberculosis is a different illness.

A story can make those facts easier to remember because they are tied to a person and a day. You may forget a lonely list. You are more likely to remember that the bottle was pulled away and that the nurse corrected the fear.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Why we read narratives — Ways to keep what you read
studyPages.body:
### Ways to keep what you read
- Retell the story in five sentences, one for each stage.
- Write three new words and use each one in a sentence that is not copied from the book.
- Ask one factual question and one inference question, then answer both.
- Talk about the story in a reading club. Listen to other readers. Their favourite moment may not be yours, and that is useful.

If you read the narrative on a screen, stay on the text your teacher has opened. Do not type a classmate's name or health into a chat, a comment or a message. This story is made up. A real person's health is private.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Why we read narratives — Example 1
studyPages.body:
### Respect while you talk
Kind discussion sounds like this: I think Amina wanted a friend, because she asked to sit down on Monday. It does not sound like a joke about illness. Love, in this lesson, is practical. It is a seat saved, an apology said, and a promise kept.

Reading is worth the effort when it leaves you better informed and more able to treat people fairly. Close the book and ask, What do I know now that I did not know at the title? If you can answer, the reading has done its work.

## Key words
• retell — to tell a story again in your own words and in the right order
• reading club — a group that meets to read and talk about texts
• private — not for public talk or for posting online

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Give one fact and one feeling a reader can take from the narrative.

Working:
1. A fact is something the nurse states.
2. A feeling is shown by what a character does.

Answer: Fact: HIV is not passed by sharing a cup or a bottle. Feeling: Amina was hurt when she heard the boys, because she ate alone.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Why we read narratives — Five sentences and a promise
studyPages.body:
## Worked examples

### Example 2
Why is it wrong to post a classmate's health online after a lesson like this?

Working:
1. Health is private.
2. The class story was a warning against gossip.

Answer: A person's health is private. Posting it would spread gossip, which the story shows can hurt someone.

## Activity: Five sentences and a promise
You will need: The narrative, in print or on a screen the teacher has chosen, Exercise books

1. With a partner, retell the story in five sentences, using Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, after the talk and Friday.

2. Each learner writes one new sentence using the word promise and one using the word virus.

3. In a small group, share what you enjoyed in the story and one fact you will remember. Listen without interrupting.

4. Agree on one way your own class can welcome a new learner.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Why we read narratives — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. Give two reasons to read a narrative.

2. How can a story help you remember a fact?

3. What should you not type online after reading this story?

4. What question can you ask yourself to check that reading was useful?

## Answers to practice

1. For enjoyment and for information.

2. The fact is tied to a character and an event, so it is easier to recall than a bare list.

3. A real classmate's name or health, or gossip about a person's illness.

4. What do I know now that I did not know before I read the title?

## Summary
• Narratives give enjoyment and information together.
• Retelling, new sentences and careful talk help you remember.
• Real people's health is private and is not material for jokes or posts.

studyPages.title: Revision quiz
studyPages.body:
REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. How many words is the narrative A Place at the Desk?
   A. About 60
   B. About 120
   C. 320
   D. 3,000

2. Where did Amina eat lunch on Tuesday?
   A. Beside the narrator
   B. Alone under the tree
   C. In the nurse's room
   D. At the tap with the two boys

3. What did Sister Wairimu say about a cure for HIV?
   A. There is no cure yet
   B. A special fruit is the cure
   C. A haircut is the cure
   D. Sharing a bottle cures it

4. Tuberculosis in the story is ________.
   A. another name for HIV
   B. a different illness that needs its own medicine
   C. a kind of razor
   D. a game

5. Why did Amina eat alone? The best answer uses a clue.
   A. The story says she was not hungry
   B. She heard unkind talk and no longer felt included
   C. The nurse told her to sit under the tree
   D. She wanted to read a chart

6. Which event happened first?
   A. The class wrote a promise
   B. Amina joined the class
   C. Sister Wairimu brought a chart
   D. The narrator apologised

7. It is unfair to decide that Amina has HIV because ________.
   A. the story says so in the first line
   B. the story never says that, and you cannot tell by looking
   C. she skipped faster than anyone
   D. her auntie takes medicine, so Amina must be ill

8. What did the narrator do after the nurse's lesson?

9. Why are narratives worth reading, according to this sub-strand?

10. What is one safe way to remember the story?

studyPages.title: Quiz answers
studyPages.body:
ANSWERS
=======

1. C. 320
   The lesson narrative is 320 words long, the length this sub-strand asks you to read.

2. B. Alone under the tree
   After she heard the boys, she ate her lunch alone under the tree.

3. A. There is no cure yet
   She said there is no cure yet, but medicine helps people stay well.

4. B. a different illness that needs its own medicine
   The nurse says tuberculosis needs its own medicine and that a cough does not mean a person has HIV.

5. B. She heard unkind talk and no longer felt included
   She heard every word by the door, and the next sentence shows her eating alone.

6. B. Amina joined the class
   Amina joined on Monday, before the whisper, the lesson and the apology.

7. B. the story never says that, and you cannot tell by looking
   Gossip about her home is not proof about Amina, and the nurse says you cannot tell by looking at a face.

8. The narrator apologised and asked Amina to sit with the class.
   The paragraph after the lesson begins with the apology.

9. They give enjoyment and information, and they help us understand how other people feel.
   A story can carry facts and feelings together.

10. Retell it in order, or write new sentences with the new words, without posting anyone's private health information.
   Remembering the text is useful. Gossip about real people is not.
